orient: Narrator: Lockwood, that same snowy night in 1801, stranded at Wuthering Heights. Part of the chapter is a diary scribbled in old books by a girl named Catherine about 25 years earlier, so for a while we hear her voice and step back into the past.

notes.g: A tall cupboard with shelves for storing clothes.
A box-bed: a bed enclosed in a wooden cabinet with sliding panels.
notes.n: Common in old northern farmhouses. It kept out draughts and gave privacy in shared rooms. This one is built around a window.

notes.g: The small windows in the door of a horse-drawn carriage.

notes.m: Not a cupboard for clothes. A 'closet' was any small private room.

notes.g: A name scratched again and again on the window ledge.
notes.n: Lockwood has no idea who she is. Earnshaw is the family name of the house (remember the name over the door). The three surnames on the ledge will make sense as the story goes on.

notes.g: A third version of the name, with a new surname: Linton.
notes.n: Keep an eye on this surname.

notes.g: The smell of the book's leather cover burning.
notes.n: Books were bound in calf leather. His candle has fallen against one.

notes.g: Pinched off the burning end of the wick.
A book, usually a large, heavy one.
A New Testament: the Christian part of the Bible.
The blank page at the very front of a book.
The traditional way of writing your name in a book you own.

notes.t: some quarter of a century back
notes.g: About 25 years earlier, so in the 1770s.
notes.n: Useful for the timeline: the diary comes from long before Lockwood's visit in 1801.

notes.g: Proper use (that is, for reading, not for scribbling in).
Every scrap of empty space on the page.
notes.n: Paper was expensive, so a child might write a diary in the margins of printed books.

notes.g: A funny drawing that exaggerates someone's features.
Hard-to-read writing (a joke comparing it to Egyptian picture-writing).
Catherine's brother. Her father is away, and Hindley is in charge.
notes.n: She calls him 'my brother' a little later.

notes.g: H. = Heathcliff, here a boy and Catherine's companion.
notes.n: Remember the diary is about 25 years old, so this is Heathcliff as a child.
Said a little scornfully: Joseph just had to do it.

notes.g: Gather people for a church service.
An attic room just under the roof.
I'm sure of it; I bet.
A farm boy who leads the horses while ploughing.
A sack of grain (wheat, oats or barley).
notes.m: In British English 'corn' means grain in general, not maize.

notes.g: Children's aprons worn over their clothes.
Hits me on the side of the head.

notes.tr: The master only just buried, the Sabbath not over, the sound of the gospel still in your ears, and you dare to be playing! Shame on you! Sit down, you bad children! There are good books enough if you'll read them. Sit down, and think about your souls!
notes.n: 'The master' is Catherine's father. So the diary begins after his death; earlier she wrote 'I wish my father were back again'.

notes.g: Sunday as a holy day of rest and worship.
notes.n: Strict Protestants like Joseph forbade play on Sundays.
From Old Norse 'leika', to play. 'Laik' is still heard in Yorkshire.

notes.g: The useless old junk (the dull religious books).
notes.m: In British English 'lumber' means unwanted old stuff, not timber.

notes.g: The spine or back cover of a book.
The dogs' sleeping place, here inside the house.

notes.tr: Master, come here! Miss Cathy's torn the back off 'The Helmet of Salvation', and Heathcliff's kicked his foot into the first part of 'The Broad Way to Destruction'! It's truly shocking that you let them carry on like this. Ugh! The old master would have given them a proper thrashing, but he's gone!

notes.g: The title of a religious book (invented by Brontë).
notes.n: Joseph's books sound like real Puritan sermons of the time. 'The helmet of salvation' comes from the Bible (Ephesians 6:17).

notes.g: 'The Broad Way to Destruction': another religious book title.
notes.n: From Jesus's words that 'broad is the way, that leadeth to destruction' (Matthew 7:13).

notes.g: The old man: the late master, Catherine's father.

notes.n: Also a joke: 'Advent' is the season of waiting for Christ's coming, but they are waiting for the devil.

notes.g: Take (without asking) the cloak of the woman who works in the dairy.
notes.n: The dairywoman milked cows and made butter and cheese.
Joseph said the devil would come for them; if they vanish, he might think it happened.

notes.g: From the handwriting to the printed text.
From the Bible: how many times you must forgive.
notes.n: In Matthew 18:21–22, Peter asks Jesus if he should forgive someone seven times. Jesus says 'seventy times seven'. So the 'First of the Seventy-First' would be the 491st sin, the one beyond forgiveness.

notes.g: An invented preacher whose sermon title Lockwood reads just before falling asleep.

notes.n: 'Sough' is a northern word for a boggy hollow or a drainage channel.

notes.g: The walking stick carried by a religious pilgrim.
notes.n: In the dream Joseph insists Lockwood can't get home without one.

notes.g: Formally thrown out of the church.

notes.n: Peat bogs really can preserve bodies for centuries.
Twenty pounds a year was very poor pay for a clergyman, even then.

notes.m: 'Determine' here has an old sense of 'come to an end, end up'.
notes.n: A joke: the two-room house is falling down into one.

notes.g: His congregation (a minister is a 'shepherd' of his 'flock').
A church post and the income that comes with it.
The main points or sections of your sermon.

notes.t: the place which knows him may know him no more
notes.n: An echo of the Bible (Job 7:10; Psalm 103:16): a person's home will no longer know them after death.

notes.g: 'You are the man!' From the Bible.
notes.n: The prophet Nathan's words when accusing King David of his sin (2 Samuel 12:7).

notes.t: didst thou gapingly contort thy visage
notes.g: Did you twist your face in yawns.
notes.n: 'Visage' means face. The preacher speaks in old Bible-style English (thou, didst, thy).

notes.g: Think it over seriously; consult my conscience.
Brothers; fellow members of the church.

notes.t: execute upon him the judgment written
notes.g: Carry out on him the punishment the scriptures prescribe.
notes.n: Echoing Psalm 149:9: 'To execute upon them the judgment written: this honour have all his saints.'
'Staves' is a plural of 'staff'.

notes.m: Usually a sconce is a wall candle-holder, but it was also joking slang for the head.

notes.t: every man’s hand was against his neighbour
notes.n: An echo of the Bible (Genesis 16:12).

notes.g: A window made of small panes of glass set in a criss-cross frame.

notes.n: A 'casement' is a window that opens on hinges like a door; a 'hasp' is its catch.

notes.g: Fixed solid with metal into the loop it should hook into.
notes.n: So the window can't be opened. Lockwood noticed this while awake.

notes.m: 'Gripe' is an old word for grip, not a complaint.

notes.g: A homeless, lost or abandoned child.

notes.m: 'Ideal' here means 'existing only as an idea', not 'perfect'. His yell was real, not part of the dream.

notes.g: Heathcliff's voice and way of speaking.

notes.n: A comically medical phrase: Heathcliff is clenching his jaw to keep control.

notes.t: You have reason in shutting it up
notes.g: You're right to keep it shut.
notes.n: Like the French 'vous avez raison'.

notes.g: In folklore, a fairy child secretly swapped for a human baby.
notes.n: Lockwood is saying the girl must have been unnatural, not really human.

notes.t: walking the earth these twenty years
notes.g: Wandering as a ghost for twenty years.
notes.n: Lockwood is being flippant, unaware of how this sounds to Heathcliff.

notes.g: Deadly sins (sins serious enough to damn the soul).
Likely to send me to sleep.
notes.m: 'Calculated to' means 'suited to, likely to', not 'planned'.

notes.g: Took on the form of a person.
Broken, interrupted breathing (as when holding back sobs).

notes.t: dashing a tear from his eyes

notes.m: Here a time word ('immediately'), not 'in a straight line'.

notes.g: Contradicted; gave a false picture of.
The good sense he seemed to have.
The embers pushed into a tight heap, to keep the fire alive overnight.
Streaked or patterned with darker colour.
A traditional name for a cat, especially an old one.
notes.n: One of the witches' familiars in Shakespeare's Macbeth is called Graymalkin.

notes.g: The iron bars of the fire grate.

notes.n: Ironic: Hareton's 'prayer' is a string of curses.

notes.g: A grunt; a noise that isn't a word.
Into the main living room, which is called 'the house' (see Chapter I).
A hand-pumped device that blows air onto a fire to make it burn brighter.

notes.n: Books of the time replaced swear words with '—', as Brontë does here. Lockwood jokes that the word is as harmless as 'duck' or 'sheep'.

notes.g: An insult for a woman: a worthless hussy.
notes.n: Originally a worn-out old horse.

notes.g: Ice so fine it can't be felt; the air was cold as ice.
The ridge or back of the hill.
Heaps of waste stone left from quarrying.
Smeared with white lime so they could be seen in the dark.
Mixed up, made impossible to tell apart.

notes.n: The house itself is two miles inside the park gate.
Big estates had a lodge at the gate where a gatekeeper lived.

notes.t: My human fixture and her satellites
notes.g: My housekeeper and the other servants around her.
notes.n: A callback to Chapter II, where Lockwood called the housekeeper a 'fixture' of the house.
